Sales reps are people in Application.People flagged with IsSalesperson = true. Counting those rows gives the number of sales reps.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS sales_rep_count
FROM Application.People
WHERE IsSalesperson = true;
```

Total stock on hand is the sum of `QuantityOnHand` in `Warehouse.StockItemHoldings`, which holds one row per stock item and is already measured in units.

```sql
SELECT SUM(QuantityOnHand) AS total_quantity_on_hand
FROM Warehouse.StockItemHoldings;
```

Gross margin in dollars on everything invoiced is the sum of LineProfit across all invoice lines. In WideWorldImporters, `Sales.InvoiceLines.LineProfit` already holds the profit for each line (extended price less cost), so no extra cost lookup is needed.

Credit notes: invoices flagged `IsCreditNote` would normally carry negative quantities and profit, so they offset the total naturally. I'm including all invoices, since the question says "everything we have invoiced."

```sql
SELECT SUM(il.LineProfit) AS total_gross_margin
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID;
```

Invoiced revenue before tax comes from the invoice lines. In `Sales.InvoiceLines`, `ExtendedPrice` includes tax, so the pre-tax amount per line is `ExtendedPrice - TaxAmount`, which equals `Quantity * UnitPrice`. Summing over all lines covers every invoice to date. Any credit notes, if they exist, carry negative amounts and net off automatically.

```sql
SELECT SUM(il.ExtendedPrice - il.TaxAmount) AS total_invoiced_revenue_before_tax
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate <= CURRENT_DATE;
```

Accounts receivable is the amount customers still owe. In `Sales.CustomerTransactions`, `OutstandingBalance` holds the unpaid amount on each transaction. It is zero for fully settled invoices and for payments, so summing it across all rows gives the total owed.

```sql
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(OutstandingBalance), 0) AS total_accounts_receivable
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions;
```

Confirmed delivery time is stored on Sales.Invoices (ConfirmedDeliveryTime), linked to orders via OrderID. The expected delivery date is on Sales.Orders. An order may have more than one invoice (for example, credit notes), so I count distinct orders and compare the date portion of the confirmed delivery time to the expected date.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT o.OrderID) AS late_orders
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.OrderID = o.OrderID
WHERE i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime IS NOT NULL
  AND i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime::date > o.ExpectedDeliveryDate;
```

Products that need refrigeration are flagged by `IsChillerStock` in `Warehouse.StockItems`. Counting the rows where it is true gives the answer.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS refrigerated_products
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
WHERE IsChillerStock = true;
```

The amount owed to vendors is the sum of the outstanding balances on supplier transactions. In WideWorldImporters, `Purchasing.SupplierTransactions.OutstandingBalance` holds the unpaid amount for each invoice. Payments and finalized transactions have a balance of 0, so summing the whole column gives the total currently owed.

```sql
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(OutstandingBalance), 0) AS total_owed_to_suppliers
FROM Purchasing.SupplierTransactions;
```

Promotions are stored in the `Sales.SpecialDeals` table, which has the description (`DealDescription`) plus `StartDate` and `EndDate`. The query selects those three columns for every row.

```sql
SELECT DealDescription, StartDate, EndDate
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals
ORDER BY StartDate, EndDate, DealDescription;
```

Products are in Warehouse.StockItems, and their stock levels are in Warehouse.StockItemHoldings, which has QuantityOnHand and ReorderLevel. "Below the reorder point" means QuantityOnHand < ReorderLevel, so I join the two tables on StockItemID and filter on that condition.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemName AS product_name,
       h.QuantityOnHand AS units_on_hand,
       h.ReorderLevel AS reorder_point
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
JOIN Warehouse.StockItemHoldings h ON h.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
WHERE h.QuantityOnHand < h.ReorderLevel
ORDER BY si.StockItemName;
```

Orders that came up short and had the remainder moved to a backorder are those where a backorder order exists (BackorderOrderID is not null). The IsUndersupplyBackordered flag shows whether undersupply was backordered, so I'll require both conditions to be safe.

In the WWI data, BackorderOrderID is set only when the undersupply was backordered, so both conditions should line up. Using both keeps the count accurate under either interpretation.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS backordered_orders
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL
  AND IsUndersupplyBackordered = true;
```

Country of manufacture isn't a column in `Warehouse.StockItems`. In WideWorldImporters it is stored as a `CountryOfManufacture` key inside the `CustomFields` JSON text column. The query casts that column to `jsonb`, extracts the key, and counts the items where it is `Japan`. I haven't run it against the data.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS products_made_in_japan
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
WHERE (CustomFields::jsonb) ->> 'CountryOfManufacture' = 'Japan';
```

Join customers to their categories, group by category, and count customers. An inner join combined with grouping naturally excludes categories that have no customers.

```sql
SELECT cc.CustomerCategoryName,
       COUNT(c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.CustomerCategories AS cc
JOIN Sales.Customers AS c
  ON c.CustomerCategoryID = cc.CustomerCategoryID
GROUP BY cc.CustomerCategoryID, cc.CustomerCategoryName
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, cc.CustomerCategoryName;
```

Products are stock items, and "groups" are stock groups. I join StockItems to StockItemStockGroups to StockGroups and filter on the group name "USB Novelties".

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemName
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
JOIN Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg ON sisg.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
JOIN Warehouse.StockGroups sg ON sg.StockGroupID = sisg.StockGroupID
WHERE sg.StockGroupName = 'USB Novelties'
ORDER BY si.StockItemName;
```

Each supplier we carry products from is a supplier with at least one row in Warehouse.StockItems. Joining Suppliers to StockItems and grouping by supplier gives the count of products, and the inner join excludes suppliers with no products. I group by SupplierID as well as the name, since names might not be unique.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierName,
       COUNT(si.StockItemID) AS product_count
FROM Purchasing.Suppliers s
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.SupplierID = s.SupplierID
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY s.SupplierName;
```

The main contact at each supplier is the primary contact, which is `PrimaryContactPersonID` in `Purchasing.Suppliers`. That ID joins to `Application.People` for the person's full name and email address. The column is NOT NULL and has a foreign key, so an inner join is safe.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierName,
       p.FullName,
       p.EmailAddress
FROM Purchasing.Suppliers AS s
JOIN Application.People AS p
  ON p.PersonID = s.PrimaryContactPersonID
ORDER BY s.SupplierName;
```

Customers link to a delivery city through `DeliveryCityID`. Each city belongs to a state/province, and each state/province has a `SalesTerritory`. So I join Customers → Cities → StateProvinces and count customers grouped by territory.

```sql
SELECT sp.SalesTerritory,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON c.DeliveryCityID = ci.CityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON ci.StateProvinceID = sp.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.SalesTerritory
ORDER BY sp.SalesTerritory;
```

Join stock items to their holdings and colors. Inner joins to Colors drop products with no color. For each color, sum QuantityOnHand × LastCostPrice.

```sql
SELECT c.ColorName,
       SUM(h.QuantityOnHand * h.LastCostPrice) AS stock_value
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
JOIN Warehouse.StockItemHoldings h ON h.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
JOIN Warehouse.Colors c ON c.ColorID = si.ColorID
GROUP BY c.ColorName
ORDER BY c.ColorName;
```

Open purchase orders are those not yet finalized, so the filter is `IsOrderFinalized = false` on `Purchasing.PurchaseOrders`. I join to `Purchasing.Suppliers` to get the supplier name.

```sql
SELECT po.PurchaseOrderID AS purchase_order_number,
       s.SupplierName AS supplier_name,
       po.ExpectedDeliveryDate AS expected_delivery_date
FROM Purchasing.PurchaseOrders po
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = po.SupplierID
WHERE po.IsOrderFinalized = false
ORDER BY po.PurchaseOrderID;
```

Approach: join Sales.Invoices to Sales.Customers on CustomerID (the customer the invoice went to), then to Sales.BuyingGroups. An inner join on BuyingGroupID drops customers with no group. Group by buying group and count invoices.

```sql
SELECT bg.BuyingGroupName,
       COUNT(i.InvoiceID) AS invoice_count
FROM Sales.Invoices AS i
JOIN Sales.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.BuyingGroups AS bg ON bg.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID
GROUP BY bg.BuyingGroupID, bg.BuyingGroupName
ORDER BY bg.BuyingGroupName;
```

Stock movements are recorded in Warehouse.StockItemTransactions, and each row's TransactionTypeID links to Application.TransactionTypes, which holds the movement type name. Grouping by that name and summing Quantity keeps the sign exactly as recorded.

```sql
SELECT tt.TransactionTypeName,
       SUM(sit.Quantity) AS TotalQuantity
FROM Warehouse.StockItemTransactions AS sit
JOIN Application.TransactionTypes AS tt
  ON tt.TransactionTypeID = sit.TransactionTypeID
GROUP BY tt.TransactionTypeID, tt.TransactionTypeName
ORDER BY tt.TransactionTypeName;
```

Customers are stored in `Sales.Customers`, with one row per customer, and `CustomerID` is the primary key. Counting its rows gives the total number of customers.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers;
```

Application.Countries has a Continent column, so the count comes from filtering on 'Europe'. Application.Countries is a temporal table, so the current rows are the ones to count. Rows whose ValidTo is in the past live in the archive table. I'll count rows in the main table directly, since the archive holds only old versions.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS european_countries
FROM Application.Countries
WHERE Continent = 'Europe';
```

Payments to suppliers are the `Purchasing.SupplierTransactions` rows whose transaction type is "Supplier Payment Issued". Those amounts are stored as negatives, so I negate the sum to show a positive total. The inner joins keep only suppliers with at least one such payment. I haven't run this against the database, and the type name is taken from the WideWorldImporters sample data rather than from the dump.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierName,
       -SUM(st.TransactionAmount) AS amount_paid
FROM Purchasing.SupplierTransactions st
JOIN Application.TransactionTypes tt ON tt.TransactionTypeID = st.TransactionTypeID
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = st.SupplierID
WHERE tt.TransactionTypeName = 'Supplier Payment Issued'
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY amount_paid DESC;
```

Supplier names in WideWorldImporters include "Contoso, Ltd." so I'll match on the name with ILIKE to be safe. The phone number and website are both columns on Purchasing.Suppliers.

```sql
SELECT SupplierName, PhoneNumber, WebsiteURL
FROM Purchasing.Suppliers
WHERE SupplierName ILIKE '%Contoso%';
```

Approach: the stock item name in WideWorldImporters is "USB rocket launcher (Gray)", so I filter StockItems by that name and return its RecommendedRetailPrice. Using ILIKE with wildcards makes the match tolerant of minor name variations, and joining Colors isn't needed since the color is part of the name.

```sql
SELECT StockItemName, RecommendedRetailPrice
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
WHERE StockItemName ILIKE 'USB rocket launcher (Gray)';
```

Vehicle temperature readings are stored in `Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures`, with one row per reading. The question asks for readings above 4.5 degrees, so I count the rows where `Temperature > 4.5`. The question refers to a single vehicle ("our refrigerated delivery vehicle"), so no vehicle filter is needed.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS readings_above_4_5
FROM Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures
WHERE Temperature > 4.5;
```

Order lines still waiting to be picked are those in Sales.OrderLines where PickingCompletedWhen is NULL, since that column is only set once picking has finished for the line.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_lines_waiting_to_be_picked
FROM Sales.OrderLines
WHERE PickingCompletedWhen IS NULL;
```

Products are stock items, and the lead time is stored in `LeadTimeDays` on `Warehouse.StockItems`. Counting rows where it exceeds 14 answers the question.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
WHERE LeadTimeDays > 14;
```

The highest credit limit given to any customer is the maximum of the `CreditLimit` column in `Sales.Customers`. `MAX` ignores NULLs, so customers without a credit limit don't affect the result.

```sql
SELECT MAX(CreditLimit) AS highest_credit_limit
FROM Sales.Customers;
```

Orders are in Sales.Orders, and the order date is in OrderDate. I filter to 2015 and group by the month number extracted from that date.

```sql
SELECT EXTRACT(MONTH FROM OrderDate)::int AS month_number,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= DATE '2015-01-01'
  AND OrderDate < DATE '2016-01-01'
GROUP BY EXTRACT(MONTH FROM OrderDate)
ORDER BY month_number;
```

Gross margin in dollars is best represented by LineProfit in Sales.InvoiceLines, which is the profit per invoice line. I'll sum it by the year of the invoice date from Sales.Invoices.

Credit notes: in WideWorldImporters, credit notes are rare and their lines already carry signed values, so I'm leaving them in to keep the total consistent with the lines as recorded.

```sql
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM i.InvoiceDate)::int AS year,
       SUM(il.LineProfit) AS gross_margin
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM i.InvoiceDate)
ORDER BY year;
```

Invoiced revenue before tax is the sum of `ExtendedPrice - TaxAmount` over the invoice lines, since `ExtendedPrice` includes tax. I group it by year of `Invoices.InvoiceDate` and compute growth from 2014 to 2015. I have not run this query against the database.

```sql
SELECT ROUND(
         (rev_2015 - rev_2014) / rev_2014 * 100.0
       , 1) AS pct_growth
FROM (
  SELECT
    SUM(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM i.InvoiceDate) = 2014 THEN il.ExtendedPrice - il.TaxAmount END) AS rev_2014,
    SUM(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM i.InvoiceDate) = 2015 THEN il.ExtendedPrice - il.TaxAmount END) AS rev_2015
  FROM Sales.Invoices i
  JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
  WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2014-01-01'
    AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2016-01-01'
) t;
```

The query sums `Sales.CustomerTransactions` rows whose transaction type is "Customer Payment Received", dated 2016-01-01 through 2016-03-31 inclusive. I matched the type by name through `Application.TransactionTypes` rather than hardcoding an ID. I haven't run it. Payments reduce the customer's balance, so I'm assuming they are stored as negative amounts and flip the sign to report money received as a positive figure.

```sql
SELECT -SUM(ct.TransactionAmount) AS total_payments_received
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Application.TransactionTypes tt
  ON tt.TransactionTypeID = ct.TransactionTypeID
WHERE tt.TransactionTypeName = 'Customer Payment Received'
  AND ct.TransactionDate >= DATE '2016-01-01'
  AND ct.TransactionDate <= DATE '2016-03-31';
```

To get invoiced revenue before tax, I sum `ExtendedPrice - TaxAmount` over the invoice lines, since `ExtendedPrice` includes tax. I group by `Invoices.CustomerID` rather than `BillToCustomerID`, so each store counts on its own instead of rolling up to its head office. Invoices are filtered to 2015 by `InvoiceDate`, and the top 5 are taken by revenue.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerName,
       SUM(il.ExtendedPrice - il.TaxAmount) AS revenue_before_tax
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2015-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2016-01-01'
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY revenue_before_tax DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Invoiced sales including tax: sum of InvoiceLines.ExtendedPrice, which in WWI already includes tax (ExtendedPrice = Quantity*UnitPrice + TaxAmount). Group by the invoice's salesperson, filter to invoice dates in 2015, and take the top one.

Credit notes: invoice lines on credit notes would carry negative quantities if present, so summing them handles them naturally.

```sql
SELECT p.FullName, SUM(il.ExtendedPrice) AS total_sales_including_tax
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
JOIN Application.People p ON p.PersonID = i.SalespersonPersonID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2015-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2016-01-01'
GROUP BY p.PersonID, p.FullName
ORDER BY total_sales_including_tax DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Cold room readings are stored in `Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures`, a temporal table. Its history sits in `Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures_Archive`, so I count rows from both. I filter on `RecordedWhen` for February 2016, using a half-open range so the whole of 29 February is included, and keep only temperatures above 4.5.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS readings_above_4_5
FROM (
    SELECT ColdRoomTemperatureID, RecordedWhen, Temperature
    FROM Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures
    UNION ALL
    SELECT ColdRoomTemperatureID, RecordedWhen, Temperature
    FROM Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures_Archive
) t
WHERE t.Temperature > 4.5
  AND t.RecordedWhen >= TIMESTAMP '2016-02-01'
  AND t.RecordedWhen < TIMESTAMP '2016-03-01';
```

Units invoiced come from `Sales.InvoiceLines.Quantity`, summed per stock item and joined to `Warehouse.StockItems` for the product name.

Credit notes: `Sales.Invoices.IsCreditNote` marks credit notes, but their lines may carry positive quantities. In the WWI data, credit notes are rare and the question asks for units invoiced, so I'm keeping it simple and summing all invoice lines.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemName AS product_name,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS units_invoiced
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY units_invoiced DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Orders have a PickedByPersonID column that references Application.People. To find the employee who picked the most orders, I'll count orders per picker, join to People for the full name, and keep only the top one. I'll filter to IsEmployee as the question says "employee" and skip orders with no picker (NULL).

```sql
SELECT p.FullName, COUNT(*) AS orders_picked
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Application.People p ON p.PersonID = o.PickedByPersonID
WHERE p.IsEmployee
GROUP BY p.PersonID, p.FullName
ORDER BY orders_picked DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Invoiced revenue before tax comes from `Sales.InvoiceLines`. In this schema `ExtendedPrice` includes tax, so revenue before tax is `ExtendedPrice - TaxAmount`. A product counts as refrigerated when `Warehouse.StockItems.IsChillerStock` is true. The query divides refrigerated revenue by total revenue and rounds to two decimals. I haven't run it against the database.

```sql
SELECT ROUND(
         100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN si.IsChillerStock THEN il.ExtendedPrice - il.TaxAmount ELSE 0 END)
         / SUM(il.ExtendedPrice - il.TaxAmount),
       2) AS refrigerated_revenue_pct
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID;
```
